# **Lab 4 genomics**

## **Working with genomic intervals & genome arithmetic**

<br>

When stuying whole genome often time we would want to annotate and overlap the different features of the genome.
Those could be ORFs, exons, CpG islands, promoters etc..
Each of these feature can be represented with a genomic interval within the chromosomal coordinate system. 
An interval may for instance represent exon coordinates or a transcription factor binding site. 
Coordinates can also give a base-pair resolution, that could hold metadata such as  read coverage, 
or coordinates that could be associated with only certain bases such as in the case of CpG methylation (see Figure 1).

Typically, you will need to overlap intervals of interest with other features of the genome, again represented as 
intervals. For example, you may want to overlap transcription factor binding sites with CpG islands or promoters to
quantify what percentage of binding sites overlap with your regions of interest. 

Overlapping mapped reads from high-throughput sequencing experiments with genomic features such as exons, promoters, 
and enhancers can also be classified as operations on genomic intervals. Of course  overlapping sets of different 
features on the genome isn't limited to the examples above and they could be useful in multiple types of studies.

Therefore this lab you will focus on analysis involving operations on genomic intervals.

The lab will follow [chapter 6](https://compgenomr.github.io/book/genomicIntervals.html) of computational genomics 
with R.

```{r ,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 1: Summary of genomic intervals with different kinds of information'}
knitr::include_graphics('genomeIntervalSummary.png')
```

## **GenomicRanges package, GRanges and Operations on genomic intervals**

This lab will use various bioconductor packages that will aid you in working withm mapping, annotating and, 
visualizing genomic intervals. 
Lets install and load them, note that some are dependencies so no need to install independently.

```{r install packages, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
#Annotation of genomic intervals
BiocManager::install("genomation", force = T)
#Work with genomic intervals
BiocManager::install("GenomicRanges", force = T)
#visualize genomic regions
BiocManager::install("Gviz", force = T)
BiocManager::install("ggbio", force = T)

#data
devtools::install_github("compgenomr/compGenomRData")


```

<br>

Let's load the packages.

```{r load libraries, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

library(genomation)

library(GenomicRanges)

library(Gviz)
library(rtracklayer)
library(GenomicAlignments)
library(Rsamtools)
library(ggbio)


```


```{r load libraries2, echo=FALSE, include=TRUE, eval=TRUE,message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

library(genomation)

library(GenomicRanges)

library(Gviz)
library(rtracklayer)
library(GenomicAlignments)
library(Rsamtools)
library(ggbio)

```

<br>

### **How to create & manipulate a GRanges Object**

GRanges (from GenomicRanges package) is the main object that holds the genomic intervals and extra information about 
those intervals. Let's create one.

Note that the second argument “ranges” basically contains the start and end positions of the genomic intervals. This 
argument accepts input in a format created by the [IRanges package](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/IRanges.htm) and that's why we specify it as such

```{r GRanges Intro, results = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE}

gr <- GRanges(seqnames=c("chr1","chr2","chr2"),
           ranges=IRanges(start=c(50,150,200),
                          end=c(100,200,300)),
           strand=c("+","-","-")
)

```

Using the str function, we can see that the GRange object is an S4 type list.
The general data structure for BioConductor packages, which means it can be subseted with @

```{r study, echo=TRUE}
str(gr)

```

When we use the head function we see that conceptually, it is similar to a data frame.

```{r study2, echo=TRUE}

head(gr)

```

Therefore some operations like subseting using [ ] nwill also work on GRanges, but keep in mind that not everything that works for data frames will work on GRanges objects since it is an S4 type object.
```{r GRanges again with subset, results = 'show',  include = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
# subset like a data frame
gr[1:2,]

```


GRanges can also contain other information about the genomic interval such as scores, names, etc. You can provide extra information at the time of the construction or you can add it later:

```{r GRanges continued with extra metadata, results = 'show', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE}

gr <- GRanges(seqnames=c("chr1","chr2","chr2"),
           ranges=IRanges(start=c(50,150,200),
                          end=c(100,200,300)),
           names=c("id1","id3","id2"),
           scores=c(100,90,50)
)
# or add it later (replaces the existing meta data)
mcols(gr) <- DataFrame(name2=c("pax6","meis1","zic4"),
                    score2=c(1,2,3))

gr <- GRanges(seqnames=c("chr1","chr2","chr2"),
           ranges=IRanges(start=c(50,150,200),
                          end=c(100,200,300)),
           names=c("id1","id3","id2"),
           scores=c(100,90,50)
)

# or appends to existing meta data
mcols(gr) <- cbind(mcols(gr),
                          DataFrame(name2=c("pax6","meis1","zic4")) )
gr
```

To access just the metadata you can use the elementMetaData() or values() functions, they both have the same functionality:

```{r GRanges elementMetaData, results = 'show', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
elementMetadata(gr)
```

```{r GRanges values, results = 'show', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
values(gr)
```

Since your matadata is stored as a datafrae columns can also be added to it using the $ operator 

```{r $, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
gr$name3 <- c("A","C", "B")
gr
```

### **Getting genomic regions into R as GRanges objects**

Most genomic interval data comes in a tabular format (BED) that has the basic information 
about the location of the interval and might also contain additional metadata. 
Let's see how we can convert convert genomic interval data into GRanges objects by loading the CpG islands dataset 
from the compGenomeRData package.

```{r getting files, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# read CpGi data set
filePath <- system.file("extdata",
                      "cpgi.hg19.chr21.bed",
                      package="compGenomRData")
cpgi.df <- read.table(filePath, header = FALSE,
                     stringsAsFactors=FALSE) 
# remove chr names with "_"
cpgi.df <- cpgi.df [grep("_",cpgi.df[,1],invert=TRUE),]

cpgi.gr <- GRanges(seqnames=cpgi.df[,1],
                ranges=IRanges(start=cpgi.df[,2],
                              end=cpgi.df[,3]))
```

You may need to do some pre-processing before/after reading in the BED file. 
Below is an example of getting transcription start sites (tss) from BED files containing RefSeq transcript locations.

```{r tss, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE, message=FALSE}
# read refseq file
filePathRefseq <- system.file("extdata",
                      "refseq.hg19.chr21.bed",
                      package="compGenomRData")


ref.df <- read.table(filePathRefseq, header = FALSE,
                     stringsAsFactors=FALSE) 
ref.gr <- GRanges(seqnames=ref.df[,1],
               ranges=IRanges(start=ref.df[,2],
                              end=ref.df[,3]),
               strand=ref.df[,6],name=ref.df[,4])
# get TSS
tss.gr <- ref.gr

# end of the + strand genes must be equalized to start pos
end(tss.gr[strand(tss.gr)=="+",])  =start(tss.gr[strand(tss.gr)=="+",])

# startof the - strand genes must be equalized to end pos
start(tss.gr[strand(tss.gr)=="-",])=end(tss.gr[strand(tss.gr)=="-",])

# remove duplicated TSSes ie alternative transcripts
# this keeps the first instance and removes duplicates
tss.gr <- tss.gr[!duplicated(tss.gr),]
tss.gr[1:2,]
```

Reading the genomic features as text files and converting to GRanges is not the only way to create a GRanges object. 
With the help of the rtracklayer package we can directly import BED files.

```{r genomation, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE, eval=TRUE}

# we are reading a BED file, the path to the file
# is stored in filePathRefseq variable
import.bed(filePathRefseq)
```

Is is possible to automatically obtain the data in the GRanges format from online databases. 
We will use the rtracklayer package to download data from the [UCSC Genome Browser](https://genome.ucsc.edu/). 
You will download CpG islands as GRanges objects. 
The rtracklayer workflow  works like using the UCSC table browser. You need to select which species you are working 
with, then you need to select which dataset you need to download and lastly you download the UCSC dataset or track as 
a GRanges object.

```{r API calls, results = 'show', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message=FALSE}

session <- browserSession("UCSC",url = 'http://genome-euro.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/')
#mouse genome
genome(session) <- "mm9"
## choose CpG island track on chr12
query <- ucscTableQuery(session, track="CpG Islands",table="cpgIslandExt",
        range=GRangesForUCSCGenome("mm9", "chr12"))
## get the GRanges object for the track
track(query)
```

> **_NOTE:_** Not every dataset can be loaded form an online resouces, 
so it is good to know how to read data from flat files as well.

<br>


### **Finding regions that do/do not overlap with another set of regions**

One of the most common tasks in genomics is mapping and aligning reads against a reference genome.
Usually, you have a set of regions that you are interested in and you want to see if they overlap with another set of 
regions or see how many of them overlap (coverage). A good example is transcription factor binding sites determined by [ChIP-seq experiments](https://www.illumina.com/techniques/sequencing/dna-sequencing/chip-seq.html#:~:text=What%20is%20ChIP%2DSeq%3F,transcription%20factors%20and%20other%20proteins.). 
However, in these types of experiments and the following analysis, one usually onlt ends up with genomic regions that 
are bound by transcription factors. One of the standard next questions would be to annotate binding sites with genomic
annotations such as promoter, exon, intron and/or CpG islands, which are important for gene regulation. 
Let's see of how transcription factor binding sites can be annotated using the CpG islands dataset. 

First, we will get the subset of binding sites that overlap with the CpG islands. In this case, looking for binding 
sites in ChIP-seq peaks/reads. 
In the code snippet below, we read the ChIP-seq output files using the genomation::readBroadPeak() function. 
This function directly outputs a GRanges object. These output files are similar to BED files, where the location of 
the predicted binding sites are written out in a tabular format with some analysis-related scores and/or P-values. 
After reading the files, we can find the subset of reads that overlap with the CpG islands dataset using the 
subsetByoverlaps() function.

```{r peaks and subsetoverlaps, fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, results='show'}


filePathPeaks <- system.file("extdata",   
              "wgEncodeHaibTfbsGm12878Sp1Pcr1xPkRep1.broadPeak.gz",
                      package="compGenomRData")

# read the peaks from a bed file
pk1.gr <- readBroadPeak(filePathPeaks)

# get the peaks that overlap with CpG islands
subsetByOverlaps(pk1.gr,cpgi.gr)
```

For each region in the CpG islands dataset, we can count the number of overlapping ChIP-seq reads using GenomicRanges::countOverlaps().

```{r countoverlaps, fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE, results='show'}
counts <- countOverlaps(pk1.gr,cpgi.gr)
head(counts)
```

The GenomicRanges::findOverlaps() function can be used to see one-to-one overlaps between peaks and CpG islands. It returns a matrix showing which peak overlaps which CpG island.

```{r findoverlaps, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
findOverlaps(pk1.gr,cpgi.gr)
```

Another interesting thing look at would be the distances to the nearest CpG island for each TSS in each read since 
those are involve in the regulation of gene expression just like transcription factor bind sites. Oftentimes, you will
need to find the nearest TSS or ORF to your regions of interest, and the code below is handy for doing that as well.

```{r overlap distances, fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE, results='show'}
# find nearest CpGi to each TSS
n.ind <- nearest(pk1.gr,cpgi.gr)
# get distance to nearest
dists <- distanceToNearest(pk1.gr,cpgi.gr,select="arbitrary")
dists
```

Now lets plot the distances as a histogram:

```{r hist Overlaps, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
# histogram of the distances to nearest TSS
dist2plot <- mcols(dists)[,1]
hist(log10(dist2plot),xlab="log10(bp dist to nearest TSS)",
     main="Distances of CpG islands from the nearest TSSes")
```

As you can see, the majority of CpG island are ~10^5bp away from TSS, meaning that they might be involved in gene 
expression regulation in a way that's indirectly involving the binding of transcription factors.

## **Dealing with mapped high-throughput sequencing reads**

The reads from sequencing machines are usually processed and aligned to the genome with the help of specific 
bioinformatics tools. Since each mapped read has a start and end position along the genome, mapped reads can be 
thought of as genomic intervals stored in a file. 
After mapping, the next task is to quantify the enrichment of those aligned reads in the regions of interest. 
You may want to count how many reads overlap with your promoter set of interest (coverage/variant calling) or you may 
want to quantify RNA-seq reads overlap with exons (useful for differential gene expression). 
This is similar to operations on genomic intervals which you have just done. 
If you can read all your alignments into memory and create a GRanges object, you can apply the previously described 
operations. However, most of the time we can not read all mapped reads into memory, so we have to use specialized
tools to query and quantify alignments on a given set of regions. One of the most common alignment file formats is 
[SAM/BAM format](http://samtools.sourceforge.net/SAM1.pdf), most aligners will produce SAM/BAM output or you will be 
able to convert your specific alignment format to SAM/BAM format. 
The BAM format is a binary version of the human-readable SAM format. The SAM format has specific columns that contain 
different kinds of information about the alignment such as mismatches, qualities etc. 

### **Counting mapped reads for a set of regions**

The Rsamtools package has functions to query BAM files. The function we will use in the first example is the 
countBam() function, which takes input of the BAM file and param argument. The param argument takes a ScanBamParam 
object. The object is instantiated using ScanBamParam() and contains parameters for scanning the BAM file. The example
below is a simple example where ScanBamParam() only includes regions of interest, promoters on chr21.


```{r mapped reads pt2, fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, results='show', eval=TRUE}
#let's get the promoter regions from the tss subset data
promoter.gr <- tss.gr
#Let's assume that all bases up to 1000bp upstream to the tss are the promoter region 
start(promoter.gr) <- start(promoter.gr)-1000
#Let's assume that 1000bp is the end of our gene
end(promoter.gr)  <- end(promoter.gr)+1000
#Let's just focus on the 21st chromosome 
promoter.gr <- promoter.gr[seqnames(promoter.gr)=="chr21"]

#Now let's get the bam file for this chromosome
bamfilePath <- system.file("extdata",
            "wgEncodeHaibTfbsGm12878Sp1Pcr1xAlnRep1.chr21.bam",
                      package="compGenomRData")

# get reads for regions of interest from the bam file
param <- ScanBamParam(which=promoter.gr)
counts <- countBam(bamfilePath, param=param)
```




Alternatively, aligned reads can be read in using the GenomicAlignments package (which on this occasion relies on the Rsamtools package).   

```{r GA package aligned reads, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}

alns <- readGAlignments(bamfilePath, param=param)

```

## **Dealing with continuous scores over the genome**

Most high-throughput data can be viewed as a continuous score (coordinates) over the bases of the genome. 
In case of RNA-seq or ChIP-seq experiments, the data can be represented as read coverage values per genomic base
position (that's what read overlap can mean). 
In addition, other information (not necessarily obtaind from high-throughput sequenceing) can be represented this way.
The GC content and conservation scores per base are prime examples of other data sets that can be represented as 
scores over the genome. 
This sort of data can be stored as a generic text file or can have special formats such as Wig (stands for wiggle) usd
by UCSC genome browser, or the bigWig format, which is an indexed binary format of the wig files. 
The bigWig format is great for data that covers a large fraction of the genome with varying scores, because the file 
is much smaller than regular text files containing the same information and it can be queried more easily since it is 
indexed.

In Bioconductor packeges, continuous data can  represented in a compressed format, called Rle vector, which stands for
run-length encoded vector. This gives superior memory performance over regular vectors because repeating consecutive 
values are represented as one value in the Rle vector (see Figure 3).

```{r ,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 3: Rle encoding explained.'}
knitr::include_graphics('Rle_demo.png')
```


<br>

Typically, for genome-wide will be stored in an RleList object, a list of Rle vectors per chromosome. 
You can obtain such vectors by reading the reads in and calling the coverage() function from the GenomicRanges 
package. Let’s try that on the above data set.

```{r coverage, include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE, results='show'}

covs <- GenomicRanges::coverage(alns) # get coverage vectors
covs
```

Alternatively, you can get the coverage from the BAM file directly. Below, we are getting the coverage directly from 
the BAM file for our previously defined promoters.

```{r coverage BAM files, include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, results='show'}
covs <- coverage(bamfilePath, param=param) # get coverage vectors
covs
```

One of the most common ways of storing score data is, as mentioned, the wig or bigWig format. Most of the [ENCODE](https://www.encodeproject.org/) project data (a project annotating genomics and trascriptomics data) can be 
downloaded in bigWig format. In addition, conservation scores can also be downloaded in the wig/bigWig format. 
You can import bigWig files into R using the import() function from the rtracklayer package.
However, it is generally not advisable to read the whole bigWig file in to memory as was the case with BAM files. 
Usually, you will be interested in only a fraction of the genome, such as promoters, exons etc. So it is best that you
extract the data for those regions and read those into memory rather than the whole file. 
Below we read a bigWig file only for the bases on promoters. The operation returns a GRanges object with the score 
column which indicates the scores in the bigWig file per genomic region.

```{r file and convert to granges, results = 'show', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}

# File from ENCODE ChIP-seq tracks
bwFile <- system.file("extdata",
                      "wgEncodeHaibTfbsA549.chr21.bw",
                      package="compGenomRData")
bw.gr <- import(bwFile, which=promoter.gr) # get coverage vectors
bw.gr
```

Following this we can create an RleList object from the GRanges with the coverage() function.

```{r RLElist to GRanges, results = 'show', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
cov.bw <- coverage(bw.gr,weight = "score")

# or get this directly from
cov.bw <- import(bwFile, which=promoter.gr,as = "RleList")

cov.bw
```

### **Extracting subsections of Rle and RleList objects**

Frequently, we will need to extract subsections of the Rle vectors or RleList objects.
We will need to do this to visualize that subsection or get some statistics out of those sections. For example, we 
could be interested in average coverage per base for the regions we are interested in or number of variants.
We have to extract those regions from the RleList object and apply summary statistics. Below, we show how to extract 
subsections of the RleList
object. We are extracting promoter regions from the ChIP-seq read coverage RleList. Following that, we will plot one
of the promoter’s coverage values.

```{r Subset, results = 'show',  include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
myViews <- Views(cov.bw,as(promoter.gr,"IRangesList")) # get subsets of coverage
# there is a views object for each chromosome
myViews

```

```{r plot of subset, results ='show', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
# get the coverage vector from the 5th view and plot
plot(myViews[[1]][[5]],type="l")
```


We can see that most area of the promoter are covered by less than 5 reads. That makes sense concidering we are working with short Illumina reads.

Next, we are interested in average and max coverage per base for the promoters using summary functions that work on the Views object.

```{r view mean and max, results ='show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
# get the mean of the views
head(
  viewMeans(myViews[[1]])
)
# get the max of the views
head(
  viewMaxs(myViews[[1]])
)
```

## **SummarizedExperiment class: Genomic intervals with more information**

As we have seen, genomic intervals can be mainly contained in a GRanges object. It can also contain additional columns
associated with each interval. Here you can save information such as read counts or other scores associated with the 
interval. However, genomic data often have many layers. With GRanges you can have a table associated with the 
intervals, but what happens if you have many tables and each table has some metadata associated with it. In addition, 
rows and columns might have additional annotation that cannot be contained by row or column names. For these cases, 
the SummarizedExperiment class is ideal. It can hold multi-layered tabular data associated with each genomic interval 
and the meta-data associated with rows and columns, or associated with each table. For example, genomic intervals 
associated with the SummarizedExperiment object can be gene locations, and each tabular data structure can be RNA-seq 
read counts in a time course experiment. Each table could represent different conditions in which experiments are 
performed. The SummarizedExperiment class is outlined in the figure below (Figure 4).

```{r ,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 5: Overview of SummarizedExperiment class and functions. Adapted from the SummarizedExperiment package vignette.'}
knitr::include_graphics('Summarized.Experiment.png')
```


### **Creating a SummarizedExperiment object**

Next you will create a basic SummarizedExperiment object. You will first create a matrix of read counts, this matrix 
will represent read counts from a series of RNA-seq experiments from different time points. 
Following that, we create a GRanges object to represent the locations of the genes, and a table for column 
annotations. This will include the names for the columns and any other value we want to represent. 
Finally, we will create a SummarizedExperiment object by combining all those pieces.

```{r SummarizedExperiment obj creation, include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
# simulate an RNA-seq read counts table
nrows <- 200
ncols <- 6
counts <- matrix(runif(nrows * ncols, 1, 1e4), nrows)

# create gene locations
rowRanges <- GRanges(rep(c("chr1", "chr2"), c(50, 150)),
                     IRanges(floor(runif(200, 1e5, 1e6)), width=100),
                     strand=sample(c("+", "-"), 200, TRUE),
                     feature_id=paste0("gene", 1:200))

# create table for the columns
colData <- DataFrame(timepoint=1:6,
                     row.names=LETTERS[1:6])


# create SummarizedExperiment object
se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays=list(counts=counts),
                     rowRanges=rowRanges, colData=colData)

se
```

Now that we have a SummarizedExperiment object, we can subset it and extract/change parts of it.

colData() and rowData() extract the column-associated and row-associated tables. metaData() extracts the meta-data 
table if there is any table associated.

```{r extract column associated data and rows, results = 'show', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
colData(se) # extract column associated data

rowData(se) # extrac row associated data
```

To extract the main table or tables that contain the values of interest such as read counts, we must use the assays() 
function. This returns a list of DataFrame objects associated with the object.

```{r extract assaysl, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
assays(se) # extract list of assays
```

You subset using the $ operator or using [] to extract specific tables from the list.

```{r extract specific tables of assays2, include = TRUE , results='hide',echo = TRUE}
assays(se)$counts # get the table named "counts"

assays(se)[[1]] # get the first table
```

Subsetting is easy using [ ] notation. This is similar to the way we subset data frames or matrices.

```{r subset, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
# subset the first five transcripts and first three samples
se[1:5, 1:3]
```

You also use the $ operator to subset based on colData() columns. You can extract certain samples or in our case, time
points.

```{r subset $ a part of SE, results = 'show', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
se[, se$timepoint == 1]
```

In addition, as SummarizedExperiment objects are basically enhanced GRanges objects, they support all of the 
findOverlaps() methods and associated functions that work on GRanges objects.

```{r subset overlap a part of SE, results = 'show',  include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
# Subset for only rows which are in chr1:100,000-1,100,000 
roi <- GRanges(seqnames="chr1", ranges=100000:1100000)
subsetByOverlaps(se, roi)
```

## **Visualizing and summarizing genomic intervals**

Data integration and visualization is cornerstone of genomic data analysis. Below, we will show different ways of 
integrating and visualizing genomic intervals. These methods can be used to visualize large amounts of data in a 
locus-specific or multi-loci manner.

### **Visualizing intervals on a locus of interest**

Oftentimes, we will be interested in a particular genomic locus and try to visualize different variants of that locus.
 Below we will display genes, CpG islands and read coverage from a ChIP-seq experiment using the Gviz package. For the
 Gviz package, we first need to set the tracks to display. The tracks can be in various formats. They can be R objects
 such as IRanges,GRanges and data.frame, or they can be in flat file formats such as bigWig, BED, and BAM. 
 After the tracks are set, we can display them with the plotTracks function, the resulting plot is shown in Figure 5.

```{r  Genomic data tracks visualized using the Gviz functions, include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, message=FALSE}
# set tracks to display

# set CpG island track
cpgi.track <- AnnotationTrack(cpgi.gr,
                           name = "CpG")

# set gene track
# we will get this from EBI Biomart webservice
gene.track <- BiomartGeneRegionTrack(genome = "hg19",
                                    chromosome = "chr21", 
                                    start = 27698681, end = 28083310,
                                    name = "ENSEMBL")


# set track for ChIP-seq coverage
chipseqFile <- system.file("extdata",
                      "wgEncodeHaibTfbsA549.chr21.bw",
                      package="compGenomRData")
cov.track <- DataTrack(chipseqFile,type = "l",
                    name="coverage")
  
# call the display function plotTracks
track.list <- list(cpgi.track,gene.track,cov.track)
plotTracks(track.list,from=27698681,to=28083310,chromsome="chr21")
```


### **Studying genomic intervals of multiple loci**

Looking at data one region at a time could be inefficient. One can summarize different data sets over thousands of 
regions of interest and identify patterns. These summaries can include different data types such as motifs, read 
coverage and other scores associated with genomic intervals. The genomation package can summarize and help identify 
patterns in the datasets. The datasets can have different kinds of information and multiple file types can be used 
such as BED, GFF, BAM and bigWig. We will look at H3K4me3 ChIP-seq and DNAse-seq signals from the H1 embryonic stem 
cell line. H3K4me3 is usually associated with promoters and regions with high DNAse-seq signal are associated with 
accessible regions, which means mostly regulatory regions. We will summarize those datasets around the transcription 
start sites (TSS) of genes on chromosome 20 of the human hg19 assembly. We will first read the genes and extract the 
region around the TSS, 500bp upstream and downstream. We will then create a matrix of ChIP-seq scores for those 
regions. Each row will represent a region around a specific TSS and columns will be the scores per base. We will then 
plot average enrichment values around the TSS of genes on chromosome 20.

```{r loci, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, message=FALSE}
# get transcription start sites on chr20
#library(genomation)
transcriptFile <- system.file("extdata",
                      "refseq.hg19.chr20.bed",
                      package="compGenomRData")
feat <- readTranscriptFeatures(transcriptFile,
                            remove.unusual = TRUE,
                            up.flank = 500, down.flank = 500)
prom <- feat$promoters # get promoters from the features


# get for H3K4me3 values around TSSes
# we use strand.aware=TRUE so - strands will
# be reversed
H3K4me3File <- system.file("extdata",
                      "H1.ESC.H3K4me3.chr20.bw",
                      package="compGenomRData")
sm <- ScoreMatrix(H3K4me3File,prom,
               type="bigWig",strand.aware = TRUE)


# look for the average enrichment
plotMeta(sm, profile.names = "H3K4me3", xcoords = c(-500,500),
         ylab="H3K4me3 enrichment",dispersion = "se",
         xlab="bases around TSS")
```

```{r loci plot,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 7:   Meta-region plot using genomation.'}
knitr::include_graphics('metaRegionchp6-1.png')
```

The pattern we see is expected, there is a dip just around TSS and the signal is more intense downstream of the TSS.

We can also plot a heatmap where each row is a region around the TSS and color coded by enrichment. This can show us 
not only the general pattern, as in the meta-region plot, but also how many of the regions produce such a pattern. The
heatMatrix() function shown below achieves that. 

```{r subset overlap, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
heatMatrix(sm,order=TRUE,xcoords = c(-500,500),
           xlab="bases around TSS")
```

```{r loci heatmap,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 8: Heatmap of enrichment of H3K4me2 around the TSS.'}
knitr::include_graphics('heatmatrix1Chp6-1.png')
```

Here we saw that about half of the regions do not have any signal. In addition it seems the multi-modal profile we 
have observed earlier is more complicated. Certain regions seem to have signal on both sides of the TSS, whereas 
others have signal mostly on the downstream side.

Normally, there would be more than one experiment or we can integrate datasets from public repositories. In this case,
we can see how different signals look in the regions we are interested in. Now, we will also use DNAse-seq data and
create a list of matrices with our datasets and plot the average profile of the signals from both datasets.

```{r Average profiles of DNAse and H3K4me3 ChIP-seq., results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
DNAseFile <- system.file("extdata",
                      "H1.ESC.dnase.chr20.bw",
                      package="compGenomRData")

sml <- ScoreMatrixList(c(H3K4me3=H3K4me3File,
                      DNAse=DNAseFile),prom,
                      type="bigWig",strand.aware = TRUE)
plotMeta(sml)
```

```{r Average profiles of DNAse and H3K4me3 ChIP-seq,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 9: Average profiles of DNAse and H3K4me3 ChIP-seq.'}
knitr::include_graphics('heatmatrixlistchp6-1.png')
```

We should now look at the heatmaps side by side and we should also cluster the rows based on their similarity. We will
be using multiHeatMatrix since we have multiple ScoreMatrix objects in the list. In this case, we will also use the
winsorize argument to limit the effect of extreme values on the distance measure used for the distance matrix.
Every score above 95th percentile will be equalized the value of the 95th percentile. 
In addition, heatMatrix and multiHeatMatrix can cluster the rows. Below, we will be using k-means
clustering with 3 clusters.

```{r multiheatmatrix, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}

set.seed(1029)
multiHeatMatrix(sml,order=TRUE,xcoords = c(-500,500),
                xlab="bases around TSS",winsorize = c(0,95),
                matrix.main = c("H3K4me3","DNAse"),
                column.scale=TRUE,
                clustfun=function(x) kmeans(x, centers=3)$cluster)
```

```{r multiheatmatrix plot,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 10: Heatmaps of H3K4me3 and DNAse data.'}
knitr::include_graphics('multiHeatMatrix-1.png')
```

These plots revealed a different picture than we have observed before. Almost half of the promoters have no signal for
DNAse or H3K4me3; these regions are probably not active and associated genes are not expressed. For regions with the
H3K4me3 signal, there are two major patterns: one pattern where both downstream and upstream of the TSS are enriched,
and on the other pattern, mostly downstream of the TSS is enriched.

### **Making karyograms and circos plots**

Chromosomal karyograms and circos plots are beneficial for displaying data over the whole genome of chromosomes of
interest, although the information that can be displayed over these large regions are usually not very clear and only
large trends can be discerned by eye, such as loss of methylation in large regions or genome-wide. Below, we show how
to use the ggbio package for plotting. This package has a slightly different syntax than base graphics. It is a
deconstructed way of thinking about the plot. You add your data and apply mappings and transformations in order to
achieve the final output. In ggbio, things are relatively easy since a high-level function, the autoplot function,
will recognize most of the datatypes and guess the most appropriate plot type. You can change its behavior by applying
low-level functions. We first get the sizes of chromosomes and make a karyogram template. 

```{r karyogram ex, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE, message=FALSE}
data(ideoCyto, package = "biovizBase")
p <- autoplot(seqinfo(ideoCyto$hg19), layout = "karyogram")
p
```

```{r karyogram,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 11: Karyogram example'}
knitr::include_graphics('karyo1-1.png')
```

Next, we would like to plot CpG islands on this karyogram. We simply do this by adding a layer with the
layout_karyogram() function.

```{r layout_karyogram CpG, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}

# read CpG islands from a generic text file

CpGiFile=filePath=system.file("extdata",
                      "CpGi.hg19.table.txt",
                      package="compGenomRData")
cpgi.gr=genomation::readGeneric(CpGiFile, 
            chr = 1, start = 2, end = 3,header=TRUE, 
          keep.all.metadata =TRUE,remove.unusual=TRUE )

p + layout_karyogram(cpgi.gr)
```

```{r Karyogram of CpG,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 12: Karyogram of CpG islands over the human genome'}
knitr::include_graphics('karyo2-1.png')
```

Next, we would like to plot some data over the chromosomes. This could be the ChIP-seq signal or any other signal over
the genome; we will use CpG island scores from the data set we read earlier. We will plot a point proportional to 
“obsExp” column in the data set. We use the ylim argument to squish the chromosomal rectangles and plot on top of 
those. The aes argument defines how the data is mapped to geometry. In this case, the argument indicates that the 
points will have an x coordinate from CpG island start positions and a y coordinate from the obsExp score of CpG 
islands. 

```{r aes, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
p + layout_karyogram(cpgi.gr, aes(x= start, y = obsExp),
                     geom="point",
                     ylim = c(2,50), color = "red",
                     size=0.1,rect.height=1)
```

```{r Karyogram aes,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 13: Karyogram of CpG islands and their observed/expected scores over the human genome'}
knitr::include_graphics('karyoCpG-1.png')
```

Another way to depict regions or quantitative signals on the chromosomes is circos plots. These are circular plots 
usually used for showing chromosomal rearrangements, but can also be used for depicting signals. The ggbio package can
produce all kinds of circos plots. 

```{r circo, results = 'hide', fig.show = 'hide', include = TRUE , echo = TRUE}
# set the chromsome in a circle
# color set to white to look transparent 
p <- ggplot() + layout_circle(ideoCyto$hg19, geom = "ideo", fill = "white",
                              colour="white",cytoband = TRUE,
                              radius = 39, trackWidth = 2)
# plot the scores as points   
p <- p + layout_circle(cpgi.gr, geom = "point", grid=TRUE,
                           size = 0.01, aes(y = obsExp),color="red",
                       radius = 42, trackWidth = 10)
# set the chromosome names
p <- p + layout_circle(as(seqinfo(ideoCyto$hg19),"GRanges"), 
                       geom = "text", aes(label = seqnames), 
                      vjust = 0, radius = 55, trackWidth = 7,
                      size=3) 

# display the plot
p
```

```{r circo plot,echo=FALSE, out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', eval = TRUE, fig.cap = 'FIGURE 14: Circos plot for CpG island scores'}
knitr::include_graphics('circosCpG-1.png')
```
